C0.quote: Bribery in an election is one of the well-studied control problems
C0.note: Computational complexity of a bribery variant for single-winner voting rules.

C1.quote: We provide a comprehensive complexity theoretic landscape of the safe bribery
C1.note: Results are polynomial-time algorithms and hardness results for bribery problems.

C2.1.value: preference order (vote); n-voter preference profile; bribed profile

C2.2.quote: (vote) ≻i , which is a linear order over C.

C2.3.note: Preferences are attributed to voters, but they are identified with the vote.

C2.4.quote: Each voter vi has a preference order (vote) ≻i
C2.4.note: The preference order is equated with the vote by notation, with no statement about reporting. The bribed profile Q is described as altered votes, not as a held attitude.

C3.1.quote: does not follow the briber’s suggestion but casts their original votes
C3.1.note: Every main analysis concerns bribed profiles Q in which bribed voters may submit votes different from their preference order P. The deviation is induced by the briber, not by voters' own strategising.

C4.1.note: No utility, welfare or satisfaction notions are used for voters. Costs are the briber's payments.

C4.2.note: The term dichotomous preferences is not used.

C5.1.note: Results concern safety and success for the briber only.

VOT.quote_behav: some subset of voters follows the briber’s recommendation exactly
VOT.note: Bribed voters follow, partially follow or ignore the briber. Safety must hold for every such subset, so voter behaviour is exogenous rather than optimising.

BRI.quote_behav: the goal of the briber is to ask the bribed voters
BRI.quote_info: we assume that the briber is aware of the votes cast
BRI.note: The briber also lacks knowledge of which voters will comply (p.714).

C7.1.quote: the briber can never be sure that the voters will eventually
C7.1.note: The briber (BRI) is STRAT; voters (VOT) are NONSTRAT.

C7.2.note: The campaigning argument motivates uncertain compliance and the worst-case safety notion. It does not argue why voters are modelled as non-optimising while the briber optimises.

C9.1.note: The conclusion's claims concern computational overhead for the briber, and the campaigning remark is motivation. There are no claims about institutions, voter welfare or rule choice.

C3.1.reason: Read literally, C3.1 asks whether any analysis has voters submitting inputs that differ from their held preference P, and every problem in the paper involves bribed voters casting Q different from P.

C3.2.reason: Since C3.1 = ALL, the codebook requires NA for C3.2.

C7.2.reason: The paper's argument justifies robustness to non-compliance, not the difference between a strategic briber and non-strategic voters, so no reason is given.

C8.2.reason: The solution concept, a decision problem asking whether a goal-achieving bribery exists, is explicitly named and formally defined as Safe $Bribery and Safe Shift Bribery.

C9.1.reason: The conclusion's statement about the briber's computational overhead is not a claim about real institutions, voters' well-being or which rule to use.
